passages.name: True Start
passages.source_raw:
The Shinkansen pulls into Tokyo Station and I press my forehead against the window. The city sprawls beyond the glass — a concrete ocean that stretches past the horizon, dwarfing every building I've ever known in Kyoto. My reflection stares back at me: eighteen years old, a duffel bag between my feet, a transfer notice folded in my jacket pocket, and a knot in my stomach that hasn't loosened since Mom drove me to Kyoto Station this morning. <>My name is <> <>.<> I'm nobody special. Quiet kid from a quiet neighborhood in Kyoto. No clubs, no girlfriend, no particular ambitions beyond getting through each day without drawing attention. The school counselor called me "socially withdrawn." My mother called it "an opportunity for a fresh start" and bought me a one-way bullet train ticket. The official story: I'm here to prepare for the Tokyo National University entrance exam. Better schools, better chances, better future. I'll be living with my aunt — Ririko Kinoshita, my mother's younger sister — in a house I haven't visited since I was twelve. The real story is more complicated. But I won't understand that until later. For now, I'm just a small-town boy stepping onto a platform that smells like diesel and rain, looking for a woman I barely remember in a city that doesn't know my name. <>
<>Find Aunt Ririko<>" "intro 1">><>
<>

passages.name: intro 1
passages.source_raw:
<><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>She's waiting at the park entrance near the station, exactly where she said she'd be. I almost don't recognize her — the last time I saw Aunt Ririko I was twelve, and she was a voice on the phone at New Year's for the six years after that. She's leaning against the railing, scrolling her phone, wearing a light cardigan over a sundress that moves in the spring breeze. She looks younger than forty-three. She looks like someone who laughs easily and worries quietly and hasn't slept enough in years. Then she spots me. And her whole face changes. <>$firstname-chan?! Is that really — oh my god, look at you! You were THIS tall last time I saw you! What happened?! You're enormous!<> She rushes over and grabs my shoulders, turning me left and right like she's inspecting produce at the market. Her hands are warm and her eyes are wet and she smells like laundry detergent and something floral I can't name. <>Auntie... it's really good to see you.<> <>Ara ara... look at this face. You've grown into a proper young man, $firstname. Your mother must be so proud. Now come — tell your auntie everything. How was the train? Are you hungry? You're skinny. You're definitely hungry.<> She hooks her arm through mine and starts walking before I can answer, already talking about dinner plans and the room she's prepared. The knot in my stomach loosens — just a fraction. Whatever Tokyo is going to be, at least it starts with someone who's genuinely happy to see me. <>
<>Continue<>" "intro 2">><>
<>

passages.name: intro 2
passages.source_raw:
<><> <> <> <>We sit on a park bench under a row of cherry trees that won't bloom for another month. She buys me a canned coffee from a vending machine without asking if I want one — the kind of presumptuous kindness that only family gets away with. The park is quiet except for pigeons and the distant rumble of the Yamanote Line. For the first time since leaving Kyoto this morning, I can breathe. <>So tell me everything, $firstname. How's school? How are your parents? Your mother barely tells me anything on the phone anymore — just "we're fine, we're fine." That woman and her walls.<> I notice the way she says it — "that woman and her walls" — with a softness that sounds like old hurt. Sisters who love each other from a distance they both maintain. <>School's... school. I'm aiming for Tokyo National University. That's sort of why I'm here.<> <>TNU? Sugoi, $firstname! That's ambitious. But if anyone can do it, it's you. Your mother was always the smart one between us — you definitely got her brains.<> <>And your cooking, hopefully. I've been living on konbini bento and instant ramen for months.<> <>*laughing* Oh, we're fixing that tonight. I'm making the good curry — not the weeknight version. The one with the secret spice your mother still doesn't know about. You look like you haven't had a proper meal in weeks, $firstname-chan. That changes starting now.<> She reaches over and squeezes my hand once — brief, warm, matter-of-fact. The way you touch someone you've decided to take care of, whether they asked you to or not. <>
<>Walk to Ririko's house<>" "intro 3">><>
<>

passages.name: intro 3
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> <>We walk through residential streets I don't recognize. Everything in Tokyo is taller, closer, louder than Kyoto. The houses are squeezed together like commuters on a rush-hour train. Power lines crisscross overhead in tangles that look like someone's nervous system exposed to the sky. Ririko navigates it all without looking up — this is her world, mapped in her muscles. <>We should hurry, $firstname. Your parents arrived this morning — they wanted to see you settled in before they head back to Kyoto tonight.<> <>Wait, they're already at your place? Both of them?<> Something tightens in my chest. Mom and Dad in the same room, performing "happy family" for Ririko. I wonder if Ririko can see through it. I wonder if she already does. <>Of course both of them. They drove up together. Your father even brought that expensive sake he hoards — I think he's trying to impress me. Don't worry, $firstname. I'll handle them. You just focus on being here. This is your home now too.<> She says "your home now too" like it's simple. Like opening a door and stepping through is the easiest thing in the world. Maybe for her it is. She's always been the sister who opens doors. Mom is the one who builds walls. <>
<>Arrive at Ririko's house<>" "intro 4">><>
<>

But seriously, Ririko — I'm counting on you. Really. Guide this boy toward a better future than his old man managed, yeah?<> He says it like a joke but his eyes aren't laughing. For a moment — just a flash — I see something in Dad's face that looks almost like regret. Then it's gone, buried under another grin. <>Don't worry, Onii-san. I'll take good care of $firstname. We'll make sure he has everything he needs.<> <>Please do, Ririko. He's... he's my boy.<> Her voice catches on the last word. Not dramatically — Mom would never allow that. Just the faintest tremor, barely there, like a hairline crack in porcelain. She clears her throat and adjusts her posture and the crack disappears. <>I know, Nee-san. I promise. He's family.<> <>I'll be fine, Mom. Really. Auntie's already taking great care of me.<> We talk for hours after that. Or rather, Dad talks and Ririko listens with her practiced warmth and Mom adds the occasional comment from behind her teacup. The fusuma doors are open to catch the evening breeze and the conversation drifts the way family conversations do — safe topics, old memories, careful avoidance of anything that matters. By seven o'clock my parents are making leaving noises, and when they stand at the genkan putting their shoes on, Mom touches my cheek once, quickly, and tells me to eat properly. Dad claps my shoulder and says something about making him proud. They walk to the car the same way they arrived — together, apart. <>
<>Continue<>" "intro 5">><>
<>

passages.name: intro 5
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <>The house exhales the moment the front door closes behind them. It's like someone turned off a machine I didn't realize was running — the constant low hum of two people performing a marriage for an audience of one. The silence that replaces it isn't empty. It's warm, and it smells like curry. Ririko is in the kitchen. The small kitchen, barely big enough for two people to pass each other without touching. She's got three pots going and a rice cooker ticking down its final minutes and she moves between them with the easy rhythm of someone who's cooked a thousand dinners in this exact space. The curry is dark, thick with potato and carrot and onion, and the whole house is golden with the smell of it. <>Sit, sit. Eat plenty, $firstname — you're too skinny, and you'll need the energy. High school in Tokyo is a completely different beast from what you're used to.<> <>Don't worry, Auntie. I'll give it everything I've got.<> She sets a plate in front of me that could feed three people and watches me take the first bite with an intensity that's almost clinical. I eat. It's good — really good, the kind of good that makes you realize you've been hungry for hours without knowing it. <>Also — if you want to make some extra money while you're here, you can always help me and Ema at our konbini and ramen shop. We'll pay you fairly for your work.<>
She says it casually, but I notice the way her fingers tap the edge of the table when she mentions the shop — a nervous habit, maybe, or just the weight of running two businesses on her own for almost a year. I don't ask about that. Not yet. <>I'd like that. Seriously — I want to help out while I'm here.<> <>That's what I like to hear, darling. Anyway — Ema, your cousin, should be home any minute now. You two haven't seen each other in what, five years? Six?<> <>Something like that. How is she?<> <>She's wonderful. First-year at Tokyo National High School — got an honor student award last semester, if you can believe it. She's grown up so much, $firstname. You won't recognize her.<> Something in Ririko's voice when she talks about Ema — pride, obviously, but threaded through it a kind of quiet amazement, like she can't quite believe she raised someone this good. She refills my plate without asking. <>An honor student? That's incredible. I can't wait to see her.<> <>
<>Meet Ema<>" "intro 6">><>
<>

passages.name: intro 6
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>The front door bangs open like a small weather event. <>Tadaima!!<> A voice that fills the entire house. Shoes kicked off in the genkan with more enthusiasm than precision. The sound of a school bag hitting the floor. <>Speaking of the devil... Ema, come here. Look who's here.<> She rounds the corner into the kitchen and I see her and my brain does something stupid. It tries to overlay the Ema I remember — twelve years old, gap-toothed, skinned knees, always following me around like a duckling — onto the girl standing in front of me now. The overlay doesn't fit. Not even close. She's sixteen. She's taller than I expected and her hair is longer and she's wearing her school uniform with the collar loosened and she's — she's beautiful, actually, in a way that catches me completely off guard. Not the way you notice a stranger is beautiful. The way you notice a familiar thing has changed into something you don't have a category for yet. Then she sees me and the recognition hits her face like sunrise. <>$firstname?! Is that really — oh my GOD! $firstname!! You're HERE! Finally!!<> She crosses the kitchen in three steps and throws her arms around me before I can react. She hugs the way she used to — all in, no hesitation, her whole body committed to the act — except now the top of her head reaches my chin and she smells like school chalk and strawberry shampoo and the pressure of her against my chest is something I'm absolutely not going to think about. <>Ema-chan... it's been so long.<> <>I KNOW! I missed you SO much! Are you staying? Please tell me you're staying. Like a sleepover? A really long sleepover?<> <>He's not here for just a few days, Ema — he'll be staying with us for a whole year. But no more sleepovers between you two... you're both teenagers now. You'll have your own room, $firstname.<> Ririko says it lightly, but the words land with a quiet weight that none of us acknowledge. You're both teenagers now. A line drawn in the air between what was and what is. <>Booooring, Mom! ...But fine. Having $firstname here for a whole YEAR is already the best thing that's happened all semester!<> <>Thank you, Auntie... really. For everything.<> <>Finish your meal first, both of you. Then I'll show $firstname to his room.<> <>
<>Ask about Kira, my other Cousin, and Uncle Daisuke<>" "intro 6-1">><>
<>

passages.name: intro 7
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> <>Ririko slides the fusuma door open and the room breathes out at me — small and clean and ready. A desk with a computer against one wall. A window overlooking the neighborhood, where the streetlights are just beginning to compete with the last bruise of sunset. A futon laid out on the tatami with sheets so crisp they still hold the creases from folding. The room smells like fresh laundry because she washed the sheets this morning, I realize. She washed them today, for me, before I even arrived. There's a small vase of flowers on the desk. Purple and white, nothing fancy — the kind you buy at the convenience store for three hundred yen. But she put them there. She thought about what this room would look like through the eyes of a boy arriving alone in a strange city, and she put flowers on his desk. <>So — this is your room, $firstname. The computer's there for your studies, and the futon should be comfortable enough. If you need extra blankets, they're in the closet.<> <>Auntie... this is perfect. Thank you — really. For all of it.<> <>It's nothing, darling. You're family. This is your home now, for as long as you need it to be.<> She lingers at the door. One hand on the frame, her weight shifted like she's about to leave but hasn't quite given herself permission yet. She looks back at me and there's something in her expression I can't quite name — not sadness, exactly, and not just warmth. Something older than both. The look of a woman who knows what it means to have an empty room become full again. <>Good night, $firstname. Sleep well. Tomorrow's a big day.<> <>Good night, Auntie.<> The fusuma slides shut with a soft wooden sound. Her footsteps pad down the hallway, pausing once — checking on Ema, probably — and then the house settles into the particular quiet of a place winding down for the night. Water in old pipes. The tick of the kitchen clock through two walls. A car passing on the street below, its headlights sweeping across the ceiling in a slow arc. I lie in the dark in a strange room in a strange city and listen to the house breathe. The futon is comfortable and the sheets smell like detergent and the flowers on the desk are a small purple shadow in the dark. My first night in Tokyo. I thought I'd feel scared, or lonely, or at least displaced. But the curry is warm in my stomach and someone washed these sheets for me this morning and the house around me is full of people who are glad I'm here. I close my eyes. Sleep comes easier than I expected. <>
<>Go to Sleep<>" "sleep">><>
<>

passages.name: Ririko 6
passages.source_raw:
<> <18>><><><><> <> <> <> <> <><><><><><> <><><><><><> <>The kitchen smelled like miso and grilled fish. Morning light slanted through the window above the sink, catching the steam rising from the rice cooker. Ririko moved between the counter and the stove with an efficiency that came from years of doing this alone -- setting plates, wiping surfaces, tucking a strand of hair behind her ear without breaking rhythm. Her apron was tied tight at the waist, and the fabric shifted against her hips every time she turned. <>As usual, your cooking is always delicious, Aunty.<> She beamed at that -- a real smile, not the polite one she wore for neighbors. The kind that crinkled the corners of her eyes and made her look ten years younger. She leaned against the counter, watching me eat, and for a moment I forgot she was my aunt. She was just a beautiful woman in a sunlit kitchen, happy that someone appreciated what she'd made. <>I'm really happy when you like my cooking, honey. It makes all the early mornings worth it.<> Her apron rode up slightly as she reached for the overhead cabinet, and I caught a glimpse of her thighs beneath the hem of her house dress. I looked away. Then looked back. She was humming something under her breath, oblivious -- or pretending to be. <>
<>Finish Eating<>" "kitchen">><> <>Grope Her<>" "Ririko 6-1">><>
<>

passages.name: Ririko 6-1
passages.source_raw:
<> <18>><><><><> <> <> <> <> <><><><><><> <><> My hand hovered near her waist. She was close enough that I could smell the soap on her skin beneath the cooking oil. The apron string dangled loose on one side, and I imagined pulling it, letting the whole thing fall. But then I heard the creak of the hallway floorboard -- Ema's room was twenty feet away, and the walls in this house were paper-thin. <>I don't wanna do anything stupid. I could get kicked out of this house.<> I pulled my hand back and shoved it into my pocket. Ririko didn't notice -- or if she did, she was kind enough not to say anything. She just kept washing dishes, humming that same melody, while I sat there trying to think about anything other than the curve of her neck. <>
<>Just don't do it<>" "kitchen">><>
<> <><> <><><><><><> <><><><><><> <>I came up behind her while she stood at the sink. My hands found her hips before I could talk myself out of it. She stiffened -- not from surprise, but from the daylight pouring through the kitchen window, reminding her that this wasn't the safe darkness of night. <>Aunty... I can't help it. I want you right now.<> She grabbed my wrists -- not gently. Her knuckles were white and her voice came out in a sharp whisper, the kind that meant she was genuinely afraid. <>Right now? Are you crazy?? Stop it, $firstname, before Ema sees us like this!<> She was right. I could hear the faint sound of Ema's alarm clock through the wall. Morning was the worst possible time for this. I let go, and Ririko smoothed her apron with trembling hands, not looking at me. The rejection stung -- but the flush creeping up her neck told me she wasn't as composed as she was pretending to be. <>
<>She's right, It's too risky<>" "livingroom">><>
<> <> I came up behind her while she rinsed the last plate. My hands slid around her waist, pulling her back against me, and she let out a small gasp when she felt how hard I already was. The kitchen was bright with morning sun, the front door unlocked, Ema's bedroom just down the hall. None of it mattered. <>Aunty... I need you. Right here.<> She turned off the faucet. Her hands were wet and she dried them on her apron, slowly, buying herself a moment to think. Then she glanced toward the hallway -- listening for footsteps. Satisfied there were none, she leaned back into me, just slightly. <>Right now? ...Fine. But be careful, and we'd better hurry before Ema comes downstairs.<> Her voice was steady but her pulse was racing -- I could feel it where my lips pressed against her neck. She reached behind her and gripped my thigh, pulling me closer. Permission granted, with a timer already ticking. <>
<>Continue<>" "Ririko 6-2">><>

passages.name: school intro
passages.source_raw:
<> <18>><><><><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>The hallway smells like fresh floor wax and chalk dust. A cluster of students stands near the entrance — five or six transfer kids, all carrying the same expression of studied indifference that barely covers the nerves underneath. I recognize it because I'm wearing it too. A woman steps forward to address us — mid-thirties, sharp eyes, clipboard held like a weapon. She scans the group once, cataloguing every face in three seconds flat. She doesn't smile. She doesn't welcome us with warmth. She addresses us the way an air traffic controller addresses incoming flights — efficient, practiced, already thinking about the next task. <>Welcome to Suzuran High. I'm Saeko Matsushita — your homeroom teacher for the year. Before you get any ideas about this being a fresh start where nobody knows your name and you can coast: I've read all your files. I know exactly why each of you is here. Now follow me. I'll introduce you to the staff.<> <>

She's the youngest person on this side of the hallway by at least a decade, and she knows it. <>This is Saryuu Usui. Physics. She's one of the youngest teachers on staff — don't let that fool you into thinking she'll go easy on you.<> Saryuu-sensei's eyes move across our group without hurrying. When they pass over me, they pause — just for a beat — then continue. I can't tell if she noticed something or if that's just how she looks at everyone. <>

If any of you are struggling with the language requirements, she runs extra sessions after school. Take advantage of them.<> Yua-sensei gives us a small bow — unhurried, genuine. Something about it makes me think she'd be the kind of teacher who actually remembers your name after the first class. <>

passages.name: yuna intro

<> <18>><><><><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>The final stop. The door at the end of the corridor has a brass nameplate that reads 'Principal' and nothing else. The woman standing beside it doesn't need a nameplate — the way every teacher we've passed straightened up as we got closer told me everything I needed to know about who runs this building. <>Yuna Shiina. Math, and more importantly — Principal. She runs this school. She's strict, she doesn't repeat herself, and she has a memory that will outlast your excuses. That said — she genuinely cares about every student here. You just won't always enjoy how she shows it.<> Yuna-sensei regards our group with the expression of someone evaluating whether a purchase was worth the price. Her eyes are sharp, her posture is perfect, and she nods once — not at us, but at Saeko-sensei, as if to say: 'these are acceptable.' I get the distinct feeling that at Suzuran, acceptable is the highest compliment you earn on day one. <>

I've noticed you've been putting in so much effort lately, and with my mom moving to Tokyo to start her new job as vice principal at our school, it feels like everything's changing. <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <><> <><><> <> <><><> <> <> <>Ara… my favorite truant kouhai. You came. Come closer—let me see those guilty eyes.<> I step to the bed. She takes my hand—cool fingers, steady pressure—and guides it to the rail, not the sheets, like she’s already thinking three moves ahead. <>How are you? Are you… okay? And—<> <>We’re fine. Tired. Hungry. Alive. He cried like a tiny CEO and then fell asleep mid‑meeting. Efficient boy.<> She nods at the bassinet. A swaddled rise-and-fall answers me. The room feels too small for how big this is. <>I… kept my decision. I’m staying with Remu. No one knows.<> <>I know. And I said I’d live with the complexity. I will. I won’t ask you to set your life on fire for me—or for us.<> She squeezes my hand once, then releases; her eyes stay warm, unreadable in that Nagi way that scares boardrooms. <>Oh... He's a boy. I should name him <><>> <>Rules, then. For the child: no lies later. He won’t be a secret to himself. For Remu-chan: no cruelty. If you choose silence, keep it clean. Don’t make her bleed for your indecision.<> <>And… us?<> <>Us is simple. I’m still me. Flirty, shameless, terribly fond of you. After recovery and the doctor’s okay, if you knock at my door at a sensible hour… I won’t pretend I don’t want you. If you can only offer stolen evenings, I’ll accept them—on my terms: no chaos near the crib, no drama in the hall. I’m a mother now, kouhai. I can hunger and still be disciplined.<> My chest tightens. Relief and fear braid together. <>You should hate me.<> <>How tedious that would be. I knew what we were. I also know what I am: independent, solvent, and very good at keeping schedules. I can raise him without you. I can also make room for you—quietly—if that’s what you choose. I’m not here to punish youth or romance. I’m here to make sure no one drowns.<> She glances at the bassinet; her voice softens at the edges. <>Text me when exams end. I’ll be sleep‑training and forgetting to sleep. If you come by—bring decent coffee and that shameless smile. We’ll… misbehave later, when my doctor stops frowning at me.<> <>And if I never find the courage to tell Remu?<> <>Then be consistent. If you choose the lie, carry it without dropping shards. If you change your mind, tell me early. I’ll stand next to you when the truth arrives. Until then, I’ll keep the secrets you hand me, and I’ll keep the door unlocked.<> She tugs my sleeve; I lean in. Not a greedy kiss—just a brief, steady press of her lips to my knuckles. It sparks anyway. <>Go, before the nurse scolds you for loitering. Eat. Study. Text when you get home. And remember—desire is easy. Decisions are the real intimacy.<> I pick up my bag. At the door, I look back: Nagi watching me, half‑smile; the bassinet rising and falling. Tokyo hums beyond the glass like it’s keeping our secret, for now.
<>End scene<>" "streets">><>

I’m—<> She doesn’t look up from her phone. Her thumb keeps scrolling. <>Mm.<> It’s not even a word. Just a dismissive hum. The silence stretches, painfully thin. <>I was just wondering if you, uh, understood the homework? The reading was kinda…<> Finally, her eyes slide up from the screen. They’re a cool, assessing grey. They look me over once, from my unsure expression down to my slightly scuffed shoes, and then back to her phone. <>If you didn’t get it, maybe you should’ve paid attention in class instead of staring out the window. Or at Yua-sensei’s skirt.<> Her voice is flat, bored. She lets out a soft, dismissive sigh, as if my very presence is a minor inconvenience she has to tolerate. <>Look, I’m busy. Go ask the teacher. Or someone who cares.<> <>Back<>" "english lab">><> <> <>Hey, Satsuki. About that essay… do you think five paragraphs is enough, or…<> She doesn’t look up from her sketch—a surprisingly detailed, sharp-looking flower. <>The requirement is 800 words. Count your words, not your paragraphs. Basic stuff.<> <>Right, but the structure…<> <>Structure won’t save you if you have nothing to say. Do you have anything to say?<> Her eyes flick up, cold and challenging. I falter. <>I… I guess…<> <>Then go write that. Don’t waste my time with guesses.<> <>
<>Back<>" "english lab">><>

She swings her leg slowly, her eyes doing a deliberate, appreciative sweep from my face down to my waist and back up. <>The rumors are true, then. You don’t walk like a nervous virgin anymore. You walk like a guy who knows exactly what he’s doing after class.<> <>And what do you know about what I do after class?<> <>I heard about the library. And the konbini storage room. And… what was it… the roof with the shy girl from the art club? You’ve been a busy boy.<> <>Keeping tabs on me?<> <>Let’s just say I have a… professional interest in talented individuals. The classroom hums around her as she mutters under her breath, just loud enough for nearby classmates to hear. <>Hmm… tectonic plates again. Eurasian plate colliding with the Philippine Sea plate… that’s why Japan shakes all the time. Earthquakes, volcanoes—always moving, never quiet.<> <>Maps, maps, maps. If the equator’s zero, Tropic of Cancer is twenty-three north, Tropic of Capricorn twenty-three south… easy. But why do they always put exam questions on the latitudes no one remembers? Antarctic Circle… sixty-six point five south. Yeah, that one always trips people up.<> <>Back<>" "geography lab">><> <><100>><><> <>Population density… Tokyo’s insane. Six thousand per square kilometer? No wonder the trains feel like sardine cans. Meanwhile Mongolia’s like… two people per square kilometer. Two! Must feel like owning the whole horizon.<> <>Capitals quiz… Cairo, Egypt. Brasília, Brazil. Not Rio, not São Paulo—Brasília. Trick question every time. And Australia—Canberra, not Sydney. Why do they love making it confusing?<> <>
<>Discuss with her<>" "Hikaru 0-1">><> <>Back<>" "geography lab">><>
<><> <>Eh? W-what? Can I help you or something?<> Cutie? Why is she bing nice to me suddenly? <>Ahh, it's nothing Hikaru, I didn't mean to disturb you<> I grin. Her eyes dart back to her notes, then back to me, clearly flustered by the attention. <>You shouldn’t… stare at me like that during class. It’s distracting. Uhm… unless that’s your plan?<> She fiddles with the corner of her textbook, mumbling faster now. <>If you need help with the lesson, just ask. I don’t mind explaining. B-but if you’re just calling me for no reason, that’s… kind of unfair. My heart’s not ready for that, dummy.<> <>

She clutches her pen tighter, eyes darting away before sneaking back nervously. <>I-it’s just… after… um… you know… it feels strange to just say “hello” like nothing happened. passages.name: Hikaru 0-1
passages.source_raw: <> <><> <> <><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> The Geography classroom hums quietly as the teacher writes on the board. I lean a little toward Hikaru, who’s tapping her pen against her open textbook. <>Hey… which river is longer again? Amazon or Nile?<> <>Mm… tricky. Depends who you ask. Most books say the Nile is the longest, but some argue Amazon wins if you count certain tributaries. Honestly… both are huge. Bigger than you’ll ever need to swim across, dummy.<> I chuckle under my breath. She flips her notes, pointing at a scribbled map. <>Here—look. Amazon flows through South America, so wide it feels endless. The Nile runs north through Africa, feeding entire civilizations. You can’t forget that. See? Geography’s not just facts. It’s stories of how people live.<> <>Back<>" "geography lab">><>

passages.name: Hikaru 0-2
passages.source_raw: <> <><> <> <><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>Hey… Hikaru. What are you doing this weekend? Because… I was wondering if you’d go on a date with me.<> Her hands freeze. She looks up slowly, eyes wide, cheeks already pink. Then her brows knit together, nervous, conflicted. <>A-a date? With you? …I don’t know. People say things about you, you know… that you’re always around other girls. I… I don’t want to end up just another story.<> I smile, leaning against her desk with calm confidence. <>Rumors are cheap, Hikaru. If you only judge me by whispers, you’ll never see the truth. I’m asking you because I want *you*. Not anyone else. Just one quiet day together, no grades, no gossip—just us.<> <>You’re… so smooth with words. That’s exactly why it’s scary. How do I know you mean it?<> <>Because I’ve never said it this way before. And because if you give me Saturday, I’ll prove it. By the end of the day, you won’t be wondering if I’m serious—you’ll know.<> Silence stretches. Hikaru glances away, then back, cheeks glowing. Finally she huffs, puffing her cheeks as if to hide her embarrassment. <>…Fine. Just this once. Saturday. But if you make me regret it, I’ll never forgive you.<> I grin; she hides her face behind her hair, but the shy curve of her lips betrays her smile. Note: Now you can go on a date with her every weekend <>Back<>" "geography lab">><>

passages.name: Hikaru 0-3
passages.source_raw: <> <><><><><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>Um… so… where exactly are we going? I—I’m not used to this kind of thing. If you planned something fancy, you should know… I’d rather it be simple. Modest. A walk in the park, talking like this… is more than enough for me.<> I glance at her, amused by her nervous tone. She looks away, cheeks faintly pink, her steps small and careful. <>Don’t worry. No restaurants, no crowds. Just a park nearby. We’ll walk, maybe sit by the pond. Talk, laugh, just us.<> <>That… that actually sounds nice. You know, when I imagined going out with someone, I never thought of candlelight dinners or expensive gifts. Just… being beside someone who listens feels special already.<> <>I can’t believe I said yes. I was so worried, you know. About the rumors, about… what people might think. But walking here with you now, I… I don’t feel that fear. It’s weird. I feel… happy.<> <>Continue<>" "Hikaru 0-4">><>

passages.name: Hikaru 0-5
passages.source_raw: <> <><><><><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> Hikaru’s lips twitch into a shy laugh. The park entrance comes into view, lanterns glowing in the distance. She slows for a moment, looking around, then exhales like she’s letting go of something heavy. <>It’s beautiful… even before we step inside. I’m glad it’s just us. If this were in front of others, I’d probably freeze up. But here… I can talk. I can laugh. I can… maybe even let myself flirt, a little.<> Her voice wavers at the last word, but her eyes glimmer. She walks ahead, then turns back, waiting for me to catch up, her smile brighter now. <>Come on, slowpoke. If this is our first date, let’s make it one worth remembering.<> <>Continue<>" "Hikaru 0-6">><>

passages.name: Hikaru 0-6
passages.source_raw: <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>That was… nice. More than nice, actually. I didn’t expect to laugh so much. I thought I’d be stiff the whole time, but… you made it easy.<> Her voice is soft, almost swallowed by the night, but there’s a small curve to her lips. She glances up at the sky, then down at her shoes, as if embarrassed by her own honesty. <>I told you. No need for fancy places. Just being together was enough.<> <>Mm… I guess you were right. Still feels unreal, though. Me, on a date. With you. If people found out, I… I’d probably melt from embarrassment.<> She laughs nervously, hiding her face behind her sleeve. I chuckle, and she playfully nudges me with her elbow. <>But don’t get a big head, okay? One good date doesn’t mean I’ll forgive you if you slip back into your “womanizer” rumors. You’d better treat me seriously… or else.<> I raise an eyebrow. She puffs her cheeks, then lets out another laugh, the sound airy and light. <>Still… thank you. For today. I had fun. Real fun. I… want to do this again. If you’ll ask me, that is.<> <>Continue<>" "Hikaru 0-7">><>

passages.name: Hikaru 0-7
passages.source_raw: <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>Hey… Hikaru. Um, instead of going straight home… do you want to come over to my place for a bit? Just to hang out. Nothing fancy.<> Her eyes widen instantly. She hugs her bag to her chest, cheeks flushing scarlet. <>Eh—w-what? Y-your place? N-now? That’s… that’s a little sudden, don’t you think?<> <>We don’t have to do anything crazy. Just sit, talk, maybe listen to music. I just… don’t want the night to end yet.<> Her lips press together, torn between shyness and curiosity. She glances away, then back, voice barely more than a whisper. <>You’re too smooth for your own good, you know that? You make it sound so simple… and then my heart won’t stop racing.<> I smile, offering my hand. After a long pause, she slowly reaches out, her fingers trembling as they touch mine. <>F-fine. Just for a little while. If I end up regretting this… you’re in big trouble, dummy.<> <>Continue<>" "Hikaru 1">><>

passages.name: Hikaru 1
passages.source_raw: <> <18>><><><><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>A-are you sure this is okay? What if your aunt finds out? I… I don’t want her to think badly of me.<> I smile reassuringly, holding the door open. The wooden floor creaks faintly as we step inside. passages.name: Saki Class
passages.source_raw:
<> <><><><><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <><> <><17>> The corridor outside Class 2 is empty. Her desk sits vacant by the window, chair pushed in at that precise angle she always leaves it—not tucked all the way, not pulled out. Just abandoned mid-thought. <>Saki has already left the school.<> Chalk dust drifts through the last stripe of afternoon light cutting across the linoleum. The room smells like dry-erase markers and whatever industrial cleaner the janitor uses on Fridays. <>Back<>" "class 2">><> <><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>Class 2 is quieter than any classroom I've been in. Six desks, maybe seven, scattered across a room built for thirty. Afternoon sun cuts through the blinds in thin, dusty bars. In the back, Rei-sensei is tapping something on her tablet, half-glasses catching the light. And two rows ahead of me, a girl sits with her chin on her palm, staring at nothing—like she'd perfected the art of being here without really being here. <>...Hey. I'm new here. From Kyoto. Guess we're in the same class for now.<> She doesn't answer. Not even a nod. Just silence—the kind that isn't awkward because she doesn't seem to register that silence is supposed to be awkward. Then a faint exhale, barely a sigh. When she finally speaks, her voice is flat, quiet, clear. <>You're sitting too close.<> <>Huh? Sorry, I didn't—<> <>It's fine. Just… don't expect conversation. I don't do “new student bonding.”<> Her tone isn't sharp. It's just… tired. The way someone sounds when they decided three years ago that talking to people costs more than it's worth. I scratch the back of my head, forcing something that's supposed to be a laugh. <>Got it. No bonding. Just… breathing the same air, then?<> Her eyes flick toward me. Bored. But something in them catches—half a second of amusement, gone before it forms—and she looks away again. Rei-sensei's tablet makes a soft click in the silence. <>You talk too much.<> <>And you don't talk enough.<> She doesn't reply. The faintest smirk crosses her lips—there and gone, like a match struck in the dark. Outside, someone bounces a basketball against the gym wall, the rhythm fading as they walk away. She turns back to the window, and the afternoon light falls across her desk like it was always going to land there, whether she wanted it to or not. <>Back<>" "class 2">><> <><100>><><> Same desks. Same blinds slicing the afternoon into bars of gold and shadow. Saki is in her usual seat, notebook open, pen motionless. She's not reading—she's just existing in the general direction of the page. <>Rei-sensei said we'll probably have another quiz next week. Guess I'll have to study harder this time.<> <>You should.<> Two words. Full stop. She flips a page without looking up, and I'm not sure she even read the one before it. <>You make it sound so easy.<> <>It is. If you care enough.<> She leans on her palm, gaze drifting to the window. The conversation folds in on itself like wet paper. I watch her for a moment—the way the light catches the side of her jaw, the way her boredom looks graceful on her. Chalk dust hangs in the sunbeam between us, suspended and going nowhere. <>
<>Back<>" "class 2">><>
<><> I drop into my seat and she's already watching me—not with her usual studied indifference, but with something sharper. Her pen is tapping the edge of her notebook, a rhythm that stops the instant I look at her. <>…You actually got a B?<> <>Yeah. Shocked?<> <>How did you do it? Nobody jumps two grades in a month here. Did you cheat, or did someone finally knock sense into you?<> <>Neither. I just… studied differently. Guess it worked.<> She leans her chin on her palm, eyes narrowing. The suspicion on her face is the most engaged I've ever seen her—like I'd broken some unspoken rule about how things work in Class 2, and she needed to know which one. <>Studied differently, huh… Sounds vague. You make it look easy, but I can't even focus half the time.<> <>Want me to show you? After school, maybe.<> One eyebrow lifts. The ghost of a smile at the corner of her mouth—not warm, not cold, just… considering. Behind us, Rei-sensei sets down her tablet and the click echoes in the half-empty room. Saki's pen starts tapping again, slower now. <>
<12>><>Go to her place to tutor her<>" "Saki 0-1">><><> <>Back<>" "class 2">><>
<><4 >> The afternoon sun pools across our row of desks, thick and lazy, turning the dust motes into slow-motion confetti. I slide into my seat and the chair leg scrapes against the floor—loud in this room, where there are never enough students to cover the silence. Saki is already here, leaning sideways in her chair with her chin propped on her hand, watching me with an expression she would have murdered me for noticing three weeks ago. <>Took you long enough. I almost thought you were skipping just to avoid me.<> <>Avoid you? Please, I'd never survive the guilt trip.<> <>Heh… you know me too well. Maybe too well.<> She tucks a loose strand of hair behind her ear. Her eyes flick to my face, hold for a beat longer than they used to, then drift to the window like she needs the escape route. <>It's weird, though… when you're not here, class feels kind of… empty. Don't make me say that twice, okay?<> <>So you're admitting you miss me now?<> <>Tch. Don't push your luck, idiot. …But yeah, maybe I do. Just a little.<> She smiles—small, real, the kind she'd deny if I pointed it out—and kicks lightly at my chair leg. Then she turns back to her notebook, the tips of her ears going pink. Rei-sensei glances up from her tablet, looks at the two of us, and says nothing. Smart woman. <>
<12>><>Go to her place to tutor her<>" "Saki 0-1">><><> <>Back<>" "class 2">><>
<><3 >> Chalk dust catches the light from the blinds like something suspended between falling and floating. Class 2 is its usual ghost town—six desks occupied out of a possible thirty, the rest stacked with forgotten handouts nobody will ever collect. Saki sits sideways in her chair, spinning a pen between her fingers with the kind of absent precision that says she's been doing it for years. <>You're late. I was starting to think my personal tutor overslept.<> She says it without looking up. But she said it first. That's new. <>You're getting bold, talking to me before coffee hour.<> <>Tch. Don't make it weird. I just didn't want you to miss the homework check again.<> <>Sure, sure. You secretly worry about me now, admit it.<> <>Keep dreaming. I just don't like studying alone anymore.<> Her words are casual. The pen keeps spinning. But the smile that flickers before she hides behind her notebook—that's the one she doesn't know she's giving. Outside, a basketball echoes off the gym wall, and somewhere down the hall a door slams. She doesn't flinch at any of it. She just keeps almost-smiling. <>
<12>><>Go to her place to tutor her<>" "Saki 0-1">><><> <>Back<>" "class 2">><>
<><2 >> The afternoon sun filters through the classroom blinds, casting the same striped pattern across the same desks it always does. But something about the room feels different today. Smaller, maybe. Or just less empty. Saki is already in her seat when I drop into mine—notes out, pen tapping softly against the margin of a page she might actually be reading. <>You're early today. Trying to impress me?<> <>Hah. Don't flatter yourself. I just didn't feel like rushing for once.<> <>Still… nice change. It's kinda peaceful having you here before the chaos starts.<> <>You talk too much. But… I guess it's better than sitting in silence all day.<> <>Wow. That almost sounded like a compliment.<> <>Tch… Don't push your luck. But yeah—maybe I don't hate having you around.<> She glances sideways—quick, guarded—and her lips curl just enough that it counts. Then she's behind her notebook again, pen moving across the page with something that might actually be purpose. The quiet between us settles like afternoon light: warm, unhurried, asking nothing. <>

passages.source_raw: <><> <><><><><> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <> <>The residential streets narrow as we walk deeper into Mazushii. Late afternoon light stretches long across cracked pavement and low garden walls. Saki walks half a step ahead, bag slung over one shoulder, kicking a pebble along the path like she's done it a thousand times before. I keep pace without trying to close the gap. <>It's just tutoring, not a date. Don't make it weird.<> Her tone is sharp but there's something underneath it. Not warmth exactly. More like the faintest crack in a wall she built on purpose. <>You really know how to kill a guy's confidence.<> She glances sideways. The wind lifts her hair, catching the light, and for a second she looks like someone who isn't tired of everything. Then the smirk returns and she faces forward again. <>You don't really talk much about yourself, do you? Like why you're in Class 2.<> <>Why? You planning to write a report on me too?<> <>No. Just... curious.<> She doesn't answer. Just keeps walking, the pebble skittering ahead of her shoe. The silence isn't hostile. It's the kind that says she heard me and chose not to respond yet. <>Go to her house<>" "Saki 0-2">><>

<> /* Saki rock paper scissor - saki_event 4 */<><3>> The clock ticks past one. Saki's room is bright today, curtains drawn halfway, a summer breeze nudging the papers on her desk. The paint smell is fainter now, buried under fabric softener and the warm staleness of an afternoon that hasn't decided what it wants to be. We spread our notebooks across the floor again, both still in uniform from class. I've lost count of how many times we've sat exactly like this. <>Alright, sensei. What are we suffering through first? History? Math? Or are you going to make me read English until my brain melts?<> <>You pick. I'll just be here, watching the slow destruction of your patience.<> She laughs quietly. Rare, but real. Then she drops her pencil and leans back on her hands, studying me like I'm a problem she hasn't solved yet. <>Tell you what. Let's make it interesting. Rock-paper-scissors. Winner decides what happens next.<> <>Dangerous offer. What exactly does "what happens next" mean?<> <>Tch... relax. It's just motivation. Maybe I'll make you do my homework. Maybe I'll... thank you properly.<> Her eyes flick up, holding mine a beat too long before she smirks and looks away. The manga stacks cast small shadows across the floor between us. <>That almost sounded like a threat and a promise at the same time.<> <>Then you'd better win if you're curious.<> She holds out her fist, fingers poised. The tension feels silly and electric all at once. <>
